bio.en: Jake Knapp and John Zeratsky are the co-creators of the Design Sprint and authors of Sprint and Make Time; they now run the venture firm Character and its Character Labs accelerator.
bio.zh: Jake Knapp 与 John Zeratsky 是“设计冲刺”（Design Sprint）的共同创造者，也是《Sprint》和《Make Time》的作者；他们如今经营着风险投资公司 Character 及其 Character Labs 加速器。

summary.en: Jake and JZ focus on their book Make Time, arguing productivity is really about protecting one peak-attention moment a day—the 'highlight' you'd be proud to name at day's end—rather than time management. They share a ton of practical, immediately actionable tactics for product leaders and founders to spend their energy better and feel good about their days. The episode is a welcome, grounding counterpoint to hustle culture, and Lenny guarantees you'll leave with at least three things to change starting tomorrow.
summary.zh: Jake 和 JZ 聚焦他们的书《Make Time》，主张“生产力”真正关乎保护每天一段注意力巅峰的时刻——即你在一天结束时能骄傲地说出的“高光时刻”，而非时间管理。他们为产品领导者和创始人分享了大量可立刻落地、能更好分配精力并让日子过得更有成就感的实用方法。这期节目是对“拼搏文化”的一剂令人舒心的清醒剂，Lenny 保证你至少能带走三件明天就能改变的事。

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: It's not really about productivity, it's not about time management. It's really just about, look, at any given day, we're lucky if we can have one great moment where we have our peak attention and we use it well. And it's not going to happen every day, but if we have some intention around it, it can happen more often than not. The notion with the highlight is imagine it's the end of the day if someone asks you, "What was the highlight of your day," what would you say? That's the anchor of everything. That's the core, that's the foundation. Things can sometimes be a mess outside of that, and you still feel really good about your days. You still feel really good about the way you're spending your energy.
turns.zh: 这其实无关生产力，也无关时间管理。关键在于，试想任何一个平常日子，我们若能有那么一刻，全神贯注并充分利用这段专注时间，那就足够幸运了。这种状态并非每天都会出现，但只要我们用心经营，往往就能让它成为常态。关于"高光时刻"的概念，不妨设想一天结束时，若有人问你"今天最精彩的时刻是什么？"你会怎么回答？这才是万物的核心与基础。即便外界事务一团乱麻，只要能抓住这份专注，你仍能收获充实的满足感，依然能感受到自己在高效利用时间。

turns.speaker: John Zeratsky
turns.en: Yeah, I think, like Jake said, we both had always sort of been dissatisfied with the state of the productivity art, and we had big things we wanted to do. I mean, when you work in any kind of job, I mean we've both spent our early careers as designers and the job is really all about doing big projects. It's all about being able to focus, being able to spend time on the things that matter. The problem is not like what should my goal be or how should I figure out what to do with my life? They usually know, but it's very hard to actually make time for those things. (00:10:16): And I think the problem is that most productivity advice focuses on getting better and faster about doing the things that are already in front of you. So, the messages that are in your inbox, the meetings that are on your calendar, a lot of focus on efficiency, like crank through that stuff. Our perspective is basically that those are the defaults. Just like our software that we use, apps that we use have defaults, those are the defaults of life, of the companies that we work in, the culture that we live in. And so, the solution is actually to change those defaults and to really flip this way of thinking on its head. So, it's not about how do I go faster? How do I get more efficient? It's about how do I put the thing that is the most important first in my day or in my life, and then build everything else around that and accept that you're going to need to do a bunch of those little things. You're going to need to answer those messages and go to those meetings, but really, start with the idea of what's most important to you? What do you actually want to make time for?
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得正如杰克所说，我们俩一直对生产力现状不太满意，而且有很多想做的大事。我是说，无论从事何种工作，比如我们早年都是设计师，工作重心往往在于完成大型项目。这需要专注力，需要把时间花在重要的事情上。这还不算我们工作之外的追求——那些想亲自掌握的技能、想与之共度时光的人。有趣的是，我们发现当向人们谈及《争取时间》时，他们总能领会其要义。他们清楚自己想为哪些事腾出时间。问题不在于“我的目标该是什么？如何规划人生？”这些答案通常已然清晰，但真正为这些事腾出时间却难上加难。（00:10:16）我认为现有生产力建议大多聚焦于更高效地处理眼前事务。比如邮箱通知、日程安排，过度强调效率，催促人们快速处理事务。我们的观点是，这些都是默认设置。就像我们使用的软件、应用程序一样，生活、工作环境、文化环境也充斥着默认模式。因此，解决之道在于改变这些默认设定，彻底颠覆思维模式。关键不在于如何提高效率，而在于如何将最重要的事项置于首位，然后围绕这些核心任务安排其他事务。当然，你仍需处理邮件、参加会议，但首要任务应是明确对自己最重要的事——你真正想为之腾出时间的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along these same lines, we're going to talk about this kind of four-part strategy that you recommend, but a couple of things before we get into there. One is along the lines you just talked about is this insight that you had of just like willpower is never going to be enough to get you to make time for the things you want to do. And you had these two concepts of busy bandwagon and infinity pools, so maybe just talk about those two briefly.
turns.zh: 基于此，我们将探讨你提出的四步策略，但在深入之前有几点需要说明。首先，正如你刚才提到的，意志力永远不足以让你为想做的事腾出时间。你提到了“跟风忙碌”和“无限泳池”这两个概念，或许可以简要谈谈这两个概念。

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: The idea of the busy bandwagon is just this expectation that everybody's busy. And in the United States, there's kind of this thing that I think if you travel abroad and talk to people for a while, then you come back, you'll notice, which is like if you ask someone, "Hey, how's it going? What are you up to?" And they'll be like, "Oh man, I'm busy." It's kind of the default answer. "I'm busy. Things are busy." And it means, usually, it could mean a variety of things, but usually it's good. Like, "Oh, it's busy, so business is booming," or, "It's busy, I'm overwhelmed," or whatever. But busy, it's kind of the expectations that everybody's busy. And we are, I mean we are busy, but we call it the busy bandwagon because it feels like you should be busy. And it's this inner feeling caused by what we see or perceive other people are doing that drives a lot of the stress. And I don't mean to sound like I'm above it all and have figured it all out. It still drives my stress, this inner feeling that other people haven't figured out, other people are expecting fast reactions from me, all this. That's the busy bandwagon, this sort of feeling that I should be busy, that everyone else is busy. And what that does inside of us is really the core of what we have to change and figure out, this getting out of a reaction mode. The other thing that happens to us are the infinity pools. And John, do you want to describe what infinity pools are in our context?
turns.zh: 忙碌的从众心理就是这样一种期望——认为每个人都很忙。在美国，有一种现象，我觉得如果你出国旅行并和当地人聊一聊，回国后你会发现，在美国，如果你问某人：“嘿，最近怎么样？你在忙什么？” 他们通常会回答：“哦，天哪，我太忙了。” 这几乎成了他们的默认回答。“我很忙。事情太多了。” 这通常意味着各种各样的事情，但通常都是好事。比如，“哦，事情很多，所以生意兴隆”，或者“忙得不可开交”，等等。但忙碌的这种感觉，实际上是期望每个人都忙碌。我们确实很忙，但我们称之为忙碌的从众心理，因为它给人一种你应该忙碌的感觉。这种由我们看到或感知到他人行为而产生的内心感受，才是导致我们压力的主要原因。我不想显得自己高高在上、自以为无所不知。这种压力仍然困扰着我——那种认为其他人还没想明白、别人期望我快速回应的内在感觉，以及所有这些情绪。这就是忙碌的从众心理，这种认为自己应该忙碌、认为其他人也忙碌的感觉。而这种感觉在我们内心深处引发的反应，才是我们必须改变和解决的核心问题——摆脱这种反应模式。另外，我们还面临着“无限信息池”的困扰。约翰，你能在我们的语境中解释一下“无限信息池”是什么吗？

turns.speaker: John Zeratsky
turns.en: Yeah, we came up with this name because we were trying to think of endlessly replenishing fount of content. So, basically if you can pull to refresh or if it streams, it's an infinity pool. So, this is pure entertainment stuff. This is stuff that people say like, "Oh, I spend so much time on Instagram," but it's also stuff that's important and necessary and productive. Email is a huge infinity pool and it's probably the single hardest thing for the two of us to control and avoid getting sucked into. And anybody listening to this is going to, I think, understand how powerful those pools are and how effectively designed and engineered those products are to be really compelling and to be friction-free and to just make it easy for us to dive back into that pool. (00:14:15): And so, when you put these two things together, the busy bandwagon and the infinity pool, you kind of have this, it's like a flywheel, but bad. You feel like you really need to be busy, you really need to be on top of everything. And then, you've got this whole collection of apps and services and products there that are ready to pounce on that, they're ready to take advantage of that set of defaults, that cultural and internal set of defaults that you have about what you should be doing. And for a lot of people, it just sort of spins out of control. So, our view is if you can name those two things, if you can understand those two things, then you can start to deliberately change some of the defaults around them, so that you can put your most important projects, people, work first, like we talked about.
turns.zh: 是的，我们之所以取这个名字，是因为我们试图寻找一种源源不断的内容来源。所以，基本上，如果你能刷新页面或者内容在流式播放，那就是无限信息池。这纯粹是娱乐内容。人们会说，我在Instagram上花了很多时间，但也有重要且必要的生产性内容。电子邮件就是一个巨大的无限信息池，对我们两人来说，它可能是最难控制和避免陷入其中的东西。听众们应该能理解这些信息池的强大之处，以及这些产品是如何被精心设计、无缝衔接，让我们轻易陷入其中的。（00:14:15）当你把忙碌的从众心理和无限信息池这两个因素结合起来时，就像一个运转失控的飞轮。但这种感觉很糟糕。你觉得自己必须忙碌，必须掌控一切。然后，你身边有无数的应用、服务和产品，随时准备利用这种默认设置——利用你对应该做什么的文化和内在默认设定。对很多人来说，这种情况会失控。所以我们的观点是，如果你能识别出这两个因素，如果你能理解它们，那么你就能有意识地改变这些默认设置，让最重要的项目、人际关系和工作优先级排在首位，就像我们之前讨论的那样。

turns.en: I'm guilty of both these things. I feel like the reason I do some of these chats, this one in particular is it's like one-on-one coaching almost. This is going to help me stick to some of the things you teach. And I've already actually implemented a number of the things you recommend, but this is reinforcing it. And then, obviously, also helping all the listeners get better at these things. Before we get into it, one last question is just like real talk, how how's your guys' productivity? turns.zh: 我自己也犯过这两个毛病。我觉得我参加这些聊天活动的原因，尤其是这次，几乎就像是一对一的辅导。这能帮助我坚持做到你教给的一些事情。实际上，我已经实施了你推荐的许多方法，但这次活动能让我再次强化这些习惯。同时，显然也能帮助所有听众在这些方面有所提升。在我们开始之前，最后一个问题是说实话，你们的工作效率如何？你写了这本书，听起来很棒。里面有87条建议，你们进展如何？在我们探讨的过程中，我想听听你们实际在运用哪些方法，但总体来说，大家的工作效率怎么样？

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: At the top of the interview, Lenny, you asked, "What do most people get wrong when they think about this productivity, time management, whatever?" And I'll frame my answer in those terms. So, most people, I think they try to get better and faster at doing what's right in front of them. We don't change the defaults in our environment, so we can focus and spend time on these different more important things. And if you think of that sort of what do I want to do? What's my goal? What do I want to spend time on that John referred to as project A, generally the things we want to do, these project A things, they're big, they're not easy to start, they're slow to create, dopamine hits, they're non-urgent. Like boss is not asking for them if you have a boss. And generally, the tasks and activities that stand in our way that keep us from doing project A, they're small, they're medium size, it's obvious how to start them, they create dopamine right away, they're supposedly urgent, email meetings, TikTok, Instagram, news, what's on your OKRs, all these things. (00:16:47): And I know what's on your OKRs may not sound like it's a peer of those others, but in a way it really can be. So, these big things, they're at odds with these little things that get in the way that the busy bandwagon expects us to do, these things that have infinity pools built in. And so for me, right now, it's a constant battle between the Jake and the busy bandwagon and my inner feeling of how can I live up to people's expectations of me and respond in the way that I should and react in the way that I should? And then, how can I do the project A stuff, the big important stuff? A lot has changed in my life since we wrote the book. (00:17:28): The summary is every few months I need a few new experiments. I have found in what has been some trying times that the tactics and the framework that we use... Because it's kind of simple and it sort of fits with these experiences that I've had for many years doing sprints, that it works. And that if I can go back to that, that if I can create space for it, if I can think about this as it's a series of experiments, if I can look at myself with curiosity and say, "Why are things not working out?" And then try to experiment my way out of it that I'm able to. But yeah, so at any given point in time, I probably give myself a B to B-, and sometimes it's a C and sometimes it's a D, and sometimes it's an A, and I'm really plugging away, but it's totally an ongoing challenge. (00:18:22): So, I'm not going to sit here and say, yeah, just follow me with a drone for 48 hours and you'll think that's exactly how you should do things. But part of our philosophy, I think that part of the way I look at it is it can be a mess. And yet, if you can create the space for those project A moments, for your highlights, that can shape everything else, if you just have those moments. Things can sometimes be a mess outside of that and you still feel really good about your days, you still feel really good about the way you're spending your energy.
turns.zh:
采访一开始，莱尼，你问道："当人们思考生产力、时间管理之类的话题时，最常误解的点是什么？"我会从这个角度来回答。我认为大多数人试图在眼前的事情上做得更快、更高效，却忽视了改变环境默认设置的重要性，这样才能专注于更重要的事情。想想看——你想做什么？你的目标是什么？你想花时间在约翰所说的"项目A"上吗？通常这些项目A类任务宏大、难以启动、耗时漫长，但能带来多巴胺奖励，且不紧急。即便有老板催促，也不会主动要求你完成。相反，那些阻碍我们推进项目A的琐碎任务——小型、中等规模、操作简单、即刻带来多巴胺刺激、看似紧急的邮件、会议、抖音、Instagram、新闻推送等（00:16:47）——却占据了我们大量时间。（00:17:28）总结一下，每隔几个月我就需要尝试新方法。在经历种种挑战后，我发现我们提出的策略和框架依然有效。它简单易行，与我多年冲刺实践的经验相契合，确实有效。只要能回归初心，留出空间进行实验，以好奇心审视问题，比如"为何事物未达预期？"，并通过实验寻找解决之道，我就能不断进步。虽然目前评分在B-到C之间，但我始终在坚持，这确实是个持续挑战。

（00:18:22）所以我不会站在这里说，你只要按照我的方法坚持48小时就能完美复刻。但我们的理念核心在于，生活本可能一团乱麻。但只要能为项目A时刻、为你的高光时刻创造空间，这些时刻就能重塑一切。即便外界一团糟，你也能感受到充实的每一天和高效的能量利用。

turns.speaker: John Zeratsky
turns.en: And having a framework for it gives you a path back. If you're just stuck and you're looking... You're sort of grasping for hacks. You're sort of like, "Oh, I read this blog post about this thing, I'll try it." That might have some short-term effect, but ultimately, you're probably not going to stick to it. You're probably going to fall back into that place of overwhelm and disappointment and burnout. But we find that if you have a system, that you can use the system and you can return to it and continue to build on and experiment, that you can make more sustainable progress on these things.
turns.zh: 拥有一个清晰的框架能为你指明回归之路。如果你只是陷入困境、四处寻找快速解决办法……那你很可能只是在临时应付问题。比如，“哦，我读了这篇关于某个方法的博客文章，就试试看吧。”这种方法或许能带来短期效果，但最终你很可能无法坚持下去，最终又会陷入不知所措、失望和倦怠的境地。但我们发现，如果你建立了一个系统，定期回顾并持续迭代，就能在这些事情上取得更持久的进步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think a really important takeaway from these two stories you guys just shared is you don't have to do all of these things. You don't even have to do most of them. If you just do one or two, if you find one or two things that can make you a little bit more productive every day, that makes a huge dent. And so, I think it's okay to feel like, "Oh, I tried this stuff. It didn't work." I think as long as you take a couple of things away today that might be useful to you, and then just try them again in the future. If they end up not working out. Like you delete an app and then you reinstall it, I think that's okay. So, I think that's an important takeaway from this is don't feel like you're failing if you're not doing all of the things that we're talking about today. (00:20:10): But let's get into it. There's this kind of four-part framework for how to help yourself be more productive. Basically, if you could just give an overview and then we'll just talk about each of these steps one by one. So, the four parts are create a highlight, laser, energize, and reflect. So, I'll turn it over to you guys just broadly, and then let's go through each of these one by one.
turns.zh: 我认为你们刚才分享的两个故事中最重要的启示是，你不必把所有事情都做完。甚至不需要做大部分事情。如果你只专注于一两件事，只要能每天提升一点效率，那就意义非凡。所以，当你尝试某些方法却未见成效时，不必感到沮丧。只要今天能收获几条对你有用的建议，未来再重新尝试就好。即使最终失败了，比如删除某个应用后重新安装，也是可以接受的。因此，从中得出的重要启示是，如果你没有完成今天提到的所有任务，也不必认为自己失败了。（00:20:10）接下来让我们深入探讨。关于如何提高效率，有一个四部分的框架。基本上，你可以先概述一下，然后我们再逐一讲解每个步骤。这四个部分分别是设定重点、专注执行、激发活力和反思总结。接下来就交给你们了，请大致介绍一下，然后我们再逐一展开。

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: It all starts with this notion of a highlight. And highlight is, I hate to say this, it's the most powerful best part, I think of the whole process. And I hate to say that because John came up with it. It wasn't even me. But I have to admit, it's really good. And I think as folks have read the book and shared it, that's the thing we hear back from people. If you could just do one thing from this book and try this out, it's a big deal. (00:20:54): The notion what the highlight is, start your day out and you imagine it's the end of the day, you're looking back on the day. If someone asked you, "What was the highlight of your day," what would you say? What do you want to say at the end of today was the highlight of today? And you start there, just like, "Okay, what would I like to say the highlight of the day was?" And you might think about what's urgent. Sometimes the highlight is this thing that really has to happen today. Today is the day there's a big meeting, or there's this thing I absolutely have to get done for work for tomorrow. That could be your highlight and getting that done well, having good attention to that will be very satisfying. (00:21:37): But a lot of times the highlight comes from joy or satisfaction, projects that wouldn't otherwise get attention. And it also doesn't have to just be something at work. It could be people in your life that you want to spend time with, a hobby that you want to spend time on. If you want to get better at Mario Kart, having a good session at Mario Kart, whatever might be the highlight of your day. The notion is just in the morning to think, "What is it and what is that highlight going to be?" And then, try to find a block that's 60 to 90 minutes. That's just usually the rough time we think it takes to really get in the zone on something, do a really excellent job, be totally focused on it. So, that highlight, that's the anchor of everything. That's the core, that's the foundation. And you start that way, you're now trying to shape your time around that highlight, and making sure that you have your peak energy, your peak attention when the time for that highlight comes around. (00:22:37): So, laser is about the tactics you might need to actually focus on that thing. In highlight, we have a set of tactics for how to create and think about and frame that highlight. Laser, we have a set of tactics for how do you pay attention when that time comes? Then for energize, it's about having the right amount of energy to do the thing, to pay attention. My highlight for today is trying to be coherent in this podcast, so this morning I need to think about what's the best way for me to have peak energy when a podcast starts.
turns.zh: 这一切都始于“亮点”这个概念。说实话，我不想承认，但我认为亮点是整个过程中最有力的、最精彩的部分。这话我不太好说出口，因为这个概念是约翰想出来的，不是我。不过我不得不承认，它真的很棒。我觉得读过这本书并分享过它的人都这么说。如果你能从这本书中做一件事并尝试一下，那意义重大。（00:20:54）关于亮点的概念，早上开始时，你想象这是这一天的结束，回顾这一天。如果有人问你：“你今天最精彩的时刻是什么？”你会怎么回答？你希望今天结束时说这就是今天的亮点吗？你就从这里开始，问自己：“好，我希望今天的亮点是什么？” 你可能会想到什么紧急的事情。有时候亮点就是今天必须完成的任务。比如今天有个重要会议，或者有份明天必须完成的工作任务。完成这些任务就是你的亮点，专注完成这些任务会让你很有满足感。（00:21:37）但很多时候亮点来自于快乐或满足感，是那些平时不被关注的项目。也不必局限于工作领域。可能是你想共度时光的人，也可能是你想投入精力的爱好。如果你想在《马里奥赛车》里玩得更好，那就好好玩一场《马里奥赛车》。这就是亮点的概念，就是早上想一想：“亮点会是什么？” 然后试着找出60到90分钟的专注时间段。这通常是我们认为真正进入状态、出色完成任务、全神贯注所需的时间。所以，这个亮点就是一切的核心、基础。你从这里开始，围绕这个亮点规划时间，确保在亮点到来时，你能拥有最佳的精力和专注力。（00:22:37）所以，激光策略就是专注于真正专注于那件事的战术。在亮点部分，我们有一套创建、思考和框定亮点的策略。激光策略则是一套在亮点到来时如何保持专注的策略。至于能量策略，就是拥有足够的能量去做事，保持专注。今天我的亮点就是在播客中保持连贯，所以今天早上我需要思考如何在播客开始时拥有最佳的精力状态。

And if not, just being curious about it, what didn't? And adjusting and trying to think, "Okay, maybe there's another tactic I can try." (00:23:54): So, the book is like... What are there like 87 tactics in the book? There's a lot of different approaches, but the expectation is not you're going to use all of them. And the expectation is not that-
turns.zh: 太棒了，太棒了。好的。是的。如果你没有通过视频观看的话，莱尼当时用了一张便利贴，把这些方法写了下来。所以，实际上最有效的做法就是把这些方法写在便利贴上，放在你能看到的地方。比如，突出重点、激发活力、确保在关键时刻拥有足够的精力等，这些都是围绕睡眠、饮食和锻炼的策略，都是能提升心理能量的实用方法，并非什么奇招。最后一点是反思，这就涉及到科学方法论了。方法是否有效？今天尝试的策略有没有奏效？如果没有，就去探究原因，调整策略，思考：“或许我可以尝试其他方法。” （00:23:54）：那本书里大概有87种策略吧？里面有很多不同的方法，但没人指望你把所有方法都用上。也没人指望——

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: ... expectation is not you're going to use all of them. And the expectation is not that all of them will work for each person. I use different tactics than John does, and some of his don't work for me, and vice versa. But that idea of centering on a thing, focusing on it, having tactics for that, having tactics for energy, and then having some tactics to reflect and reframe and be curious. That taken together, we find, just can reframe the way it feels. It's not really about productivity. It's not about time management. It's really just about, look, in any given day, we're lucky if we can have one great moment where we have our peak attention, and we use it well. And it's not going to happen every day, but if we have some intention around it, it can happen more often than not.
turns.zh: ……没人指望你把所有方法都用上。也没人指望所有方法对每个人都适用。我和约翰用的策略不同，他有些方法对我没用，反之亦然。但核心理念就是专注于某个目标，制定相关策略，提升精力水平，再通过反思、重新规划和保持好奇心来调整方法。综合这些策略，我们发现能重新定义工作的体验。这本书重点不在于提高效率，也不在于时间管理，而是要认识到：在每一天中，如果能有那么一刻全神贯注并充分利用这段高效时间，我们就很幸运了。这种状态不可能每天都有，但只要用心规划，就能让这种时刻变得更加频繁。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that last point is so important and why the highlight works so well for me is usually there's... You don't get anything amazingly done in a day, often. And usually, you're just distracted by all these things, and you're doing all the easy stuff. You talked about this idea of Project A, like here's the thing I really want to get done, but the dopamine hit us so far in the future, and it's so hard. And so, the reason I think the highlight is so powerful is, you get one thing done you're proud of, that is a great day. And it may sound crazy that that's true, but it's so true.
turns.zh: 我觉得最后一点非常重要。对我来说，亮点功能之所以效果显著，通常是因为……你往往无法在一天内完成惊人的任务，多数时候会被各种琐事分心，只做些简单的事。你提到的A计划理念——比如我真正想完成的任务，但多巴胺带来的满足感总是遥不可及，实在太难了。所以我认为亮点功能之所以如此强大，是因为当你完成一件令自己自豪的事，这一天就算成功了。听起来这似乎难以置信，但事实就是如此。

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: Yeah, totally.
turns.zh: 是啊，一点没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, I want to talk more in depth about each of these four things, and maybe spend the most time on the highlight and the laser because I think that's where most of the impact comes from. (00:25:25): So, with the highlight, do you have any advice? You shared a couple examples of how to come up with like, "Here's the thing to pick for the day." There's a few questions that you recommend, and I think you shared a couple of them. And then, are there any examples of highlights from your guys', I don't know, past couple of weeks that would be good for people to hear an example? And then, also, there's this calendar component, which maybe fits into the laser, but I guess that feels like a really important element of this. So, if you just talk about that?
turns.zh: 接下来，我想更深入地探讨这四个要素中的每一个，或许会把最多时间花在亮点功能和激光功能上，因为我认为这两个功能带来了最大的影响。（00:25:25）：关于亮点功能，你有什么建议吗？你分享了几个如何确定当日任务的例子，还提到了几个推荐的问题，我记得你分享过其中几个。那么，你们过去几周里有没有什么亮点案例，适合大家听一听呢？另外，日历功能部分可能属于激光功能，但我觉得这部分功能也非常重要。你能具体讲讲吗？

turns.speaker: John Zeratsky
turns.en: For me, and again, this is where the framework is intentionally flexible, different people have different highlights. But for me, I am very project oriented. I'm very work oriented. And for me, most days, a really good day comes from having made progress on something that is really important to me. So, my highlights are usually focused work, creative work related. And this has become even more important since we started our own VC firm three years ago. And before that, I was sort of, I guess, more or less a writer, full-time writing, and speaking at events, and doing some consulting. And before that, I was a partner at Google Ventures, at GV, and before that I was a product designer. So, I've been through different modes and contexts in my career. But if you know any VCs, if you're listening to this and you know any VCs, they're probably the busiest, most frazzled people that you know who are constantly on email, constantly in Zoom calls and meetings, and on airplanes all the time. (00:27:08): And so, the natural environment of that work is the busy bandwagon, and it's to have a lot of infinity pools that you need to care about. And so, in that context, in order for us to make progress on projects, in order for us to move the ball on a launch related to this program, Character Labs, that we run with pre-seed founders that's coming up, or we're writing a new book, and that's a big project, or working with one of our portfolio companies and running a sprint with them, or writing a newsletter that goes out to our LPs, those things are all really important, and I feel like they give us a unique edge as a VC firm. (00:27:55): If we accept the premise I said before, that most VCs are just sort of frantically running around, if we can take these bigger swings at things, then theoretically, they should really help us be successful. So, most of the time, it's all a very long way of saying that most of the time my highlights are like, "What do I want to accomplish at work? What is the thing that I want to get done today?" (00:28:18): And so, what I do then is, I structure my calendar around making time for that. There's a tactic in the book called Design Your Day that is really about kind of drawing out your day, and using your calendar as a canvas where you can design how you want to spend your time rather than using your calendar as a thing that is done to you, a thing that tells you what you have to do. Reclaim control over that. (00:28:48): And so, most days, the first half of the day before lunch is my focus time, and I protect that very, very intensely, and then use that time to work on whatever my highlight is.
turns.zh: 对我而言，再说一次，这个框架是有意设计得灵活的，不同的人有不同的侧重点。但对我而言，我非常以项目为导向，以工作为导向。对我来说，大多数日子里，真正美好的一天来自于在对我非常重要的事情上取得进展。所以，我的亮点通常集中在专注的工作和创意工作上。自从三年前我们创办自己的风投公司以来，这一点变得更加重要。在此之前，我可以说，我或多或少还是个全职作家，参加活动演讲，做一些咨询工作。再往前，我是谷歌风投（GV）的合伙人。更早之前，我还是一名产品设计师。所以，我在职业生涯中经历了不同的模式和环境。但如果你认识任何风投人士，如果你听这期播客并认识一些风投，他们很可能是你认识的最忙碌、最疲惫的人——不断查看邮件、参加Zoom会议、频繁乘飞机出差。（00:27:08）所以，这种工作的自然环境就是忙碌的旋风，你需要关注无数的事情。在这种背景下，为了在项目上取得进展，为了推进与我们合作的初创公司相关的发布计划，比如即将推出的Character Labs项目，或者写一本新书（这是一个大项目），或者与我们的投资组合公司合作并与他们一起开展冲刺活动，或者为我们的有限合伙人撰写时事通讯，这些事情都非常重要，我觉得它们为我们作为风投公司提供了独特的优势。（00:27:55）如果我们接受我之前提到的假设，即大多数风投只是疯狂地四处奔波，那么如果我们能在更重大的事情上大胆尝试，从理论上讲，这应该会帮助我们取得成功。所以，大多数时候，这一切都可以用一句话来概括：大多数时候，我的亮点都是“我想在工作中完成什么？今天我想完成什么事情？”（00:28:18）所以，我接下来会围绕这个目标来安排我的日程。书中有一个叫做“设计你的一天”的策略，实质上是把一天拆解开来，把日历当作画布，设计你想如何度过时间，而不是被动接受日历安排的任务。重新夺回对时间的控制权。（00:28:48）所以，大多数日子里，午餐前的前半段是我专注工作的时间，我会非常严格地保护这段时间，然后用这段时间来完成我的亮点任务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We had a previous guest on, Neer Eyal, also talking about productivity, and he had actually the same advice of just using your calendar as your to-do list, basically, because that's where time's going to go, what your calendar's telling you to do. So, I think there's a pattern here that I think people need to pay attention to.
turns.zh: 我们之前请过一位嘉宾，尼尔·埃亚尔（Neer Eyal），他也谈到了生产力问题，他实际上给出了同样的建议，就是把日历当作待办清单，因为时间最终都会花在日历上告诉你要做的事情上。所以，我认为这里有一个模式，人们需要注意到这一点。

turns.speaker: John Zeratsky
turns.en: Yeah, definitely. Yeah, and I mean, we take it even further, and we have sort of a calendar template that we use as a team. So, we have certain times of the week. And it's not exactly the same for all of us on the team, but there are certain times of the week where it's like, yeah, this is when we do these kinds of things. This is when we have these kinds of meetings. (00:29:43): And not to say that those are all standing meetings, although we have some of those as well, but these are kind of the content buckets in the template that we can fill with a specific type of activity, but then other parts of the template are sort of reserved for focus work, reserved for individual, solo time to work on things that we need to get done. (00:30:03): So, yeah. I think the calendar is, at an individual level and especially at a team level, is this really powerful tool that most people just kind of... Not only do they not use it as a tool, they just sort of hate it. They're sort of like, "Ugh, my calendar, it's a mess. If I could live without a calendar, that would be the dream." But I think if you can use some of these tactics or use other approaches to reclaim it, and use it proactively as a tool for yourself, it can really help you structure your time around the things that you care about.
turns.zh: 是的，绝对没错。嗯，我们甚至更进一步，我们有一种团队使用的日历模板。所以，我们每周都有固定的时间段。虽然团队里每个人的安排不完全相同，但每周总有特定的时间段，比如说，就是专门做这些事、开这些会议的。（00:29:43）：这倒不全是固定的会议，虽然我们也有一些固定会议，但模板中的某些部分是留给专注工作的，是留给个人独自处理需要完成的任务的。（00:30:03）：所以，是的。我认为日历，无论是个人层面还是团队层面，都是一个非常强大的工具，但大多数人只是把它当作负担，不仅不把它当作工具，甚至还讨厌它。他们会说，“啊，我的日历一团糟。要是能不用日历就好了。” 但我认为，如果你能利用一些策略或其他方法重新掌控它，积极主动地将其作为个人工具，它真的能帮助你围绕自己关心的事情合理安排时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. The way I've been starting to use my calendar is this way, exactly, is I try to prepare for work on next week's newsletter post for like an hour and a half, then prep for the podcast coming up in a few weeks. So, it's very specific and broken up. (00:30:55): Along those lines, I often don't do these things as I planned. And one of your principles, something around Groundhog Day, it's okay to repeat it if you didn't do it. If you highlight you didn't do, just repeat it again and again until you do it. Right?
turns.zh: 是的。我开始使用日历的方式正是这样的，我会先花一个半小时为下周的通讯内容做准备，然后再为几周后的播客做准备。这样安排得非常具体且井井有条。（00:30:55）：同样，我也经常没能按计划完成这些任务。而你提到的关于“土拨鼠日”的原则之一，如果你没能完成某件事，就没关系。只要突出你没做成，就反复尝试，直到成功。是吧？

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: I think that what's so cool about this notion of Groundhog Day. And if you've seen the movie... Well, if you haven't seen the movie, see the movie. What a great movie.
turns.zh: 我觉得“土拨鼠日”这个概念太棒了。如果你看过那部电影……嗯，如果你没看过，那你一定要去看。真是一部很棒的电影。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It was a good movie.
turns.zh: 那部电影确实不错。

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: If you've seen the movie, you know it's like, not to give it away, but he gets better and better at doing the day, and that's kind of this core philosophy that we take on. (00:31:30): I think a lot of the time, when in the past I have thought about, "How can I be effective with my time? How can I be productive?" It's beating myself up. It's not a good feeling to be in that head space of like, "I'm screwing up. What can I fix?" (00:31:49): And this notion that it's like, you're going to have another chance, you're going to have another chance. "It's okay, just try again, just be curious about what happened," is a big deal. And starting with the calendar, using the calendar as a framework for saying, "Hey, here's what actually happened. Here's what I think is going to happen." That's what you're saying when you do this Design your Day tactic. (00:32:12): And I did this exercise earlier this week. I was switching to a new calendar thing, and trying some new features with... We invest in this company called Reclaim, and they do this stuff-
turns.zh: 如果你看过那部电影，你就会知道，影片里主角在重复同一天的经历，但他每次都会做得越来越好。这正是我们所秉持的核心理念。（00:31:30）：过去当我思考“如何有效利用时间？如何提高效率？”时，总是在自责。那种陷入“我做得一团糟，该怎么改进”的心态真的很不好受。（00:31:49）：而“你还有一次机会，你还有一次机会。没关系，再试一次，多去探究发生了什么”的这种观念，意义重大。从日历开始，利用日历作为框架，说：“嘿，这就是实际发生的。我觉得接下来会这样。” 这就是你使用“设计你的日程”策略时所传达的意思。（00:32:12）：这周早些时候我做了这个练习。我正在转用新的日历工具，尝试一些新功能。我们投资了一家叫Reclaim的公司，他们做这些东西——

turns.en: I'm an investor in Reclaim also.
turns.zh: 我也是Reclaim的投资者。

turns.en: Oh, well.
turns.zh: 哦，真巧。

turns.en: How about that? Not planned, this promotion.

turns.en: Yeah, little [inaudible 00:32:36] there.
turns.zh: 是啊，那里有点（00:32:36，语音模糊）。

turns.en: It sounds like we knew that, but we actually didn't know that. I didn't know that you-

turns.en: We did not know that.
turns.zh: 我们并不知道这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How about that?
turns.zh: 那怎么样？

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: That was just discovered. So anyway, I was just looking at my calendar, and I was like, you know what? I'm going to do what John does. When I wake up, I'm going to schedule when I exercise, when I eat breakfast. I'm going to schedule when I take a shower, everything, and block it all out. When I walk and feed the dogs, everything's going to be on there, so that then I can have this idea, and when the day starts, I know there's slots for all those things. And then I've found this week that what I thought happened, how long I thought those things take, was not how long they take. And so, set that thing to repeat every day and look at it, and then I'm like, "Oh, okay, interesting. That's not what happened." (00:33:20): Okay, so I can adjust it. I can adjust the template and be a bit more kind to myself about this part, be a bit more kind to myself about that part. Gosh, the morning time wasn't a good focus time for me. I'll see if I can... Is there a way I can make that block happen in the afternoon? It's just a helpful way to track stuff and see it. (00:33:41): Especially, I think a lot of people are visual learners. We can benefit from seeing things. It's not everybody, but a lot of us are in that camp. And when you put it on the calendar, you can see it, and that helps a lot.
turns.zh: 那才刚刚发现。所以不管怎样，我刚刚在看我的日历，我想，知道吗？我要照约翰那样做。当我醒来时，我会安排锻炼时间、早餐时间、洗澡时间等等，把所有时间都规划好。遛狗、喂狗这些事也会安排进去，这样我就能有个大致的规划，当一天开始时，我知道这些时间都被预留了。然后这周我发现，我原以为会发生的事，原以为需要多长时间，结果却不是那样。所以我把这个设置成每天重复，查看日历，然后我想，"哦，好的，有意思。实际情况不是那样。"（00:33:20）：好吧，那我可以调整。我可以调整模板，对这部分对自己宽容一点，对那部分也宽容一点。天哪，早晨时间对我来说不是个好专注时段。我看看能不能……有没有办法把这些时间安排到下午呢？这只是个有用的追踪方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And also keeps someone else from booking that time. Double win.
turns.zh: 还能防止别人占用那段时间。双赢。

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: Not to be undervalued, keeps someone else from booking that time. Right. And they look, they see, oh, okay, Lenny's already got stuff going on. I figured out, okay, I better be cautious before I ask for something. And that default, to be helpful to other people, and say yes when they put something on a free spot on your calendar, defeats a lot of our inner purposes. (00:34:20): And one core idea I don't think we've mentioned yet is that we strongly believe in people's intuition about how they should spend their time if they have the chance. What really is important. And that is true. We're talking about running this VC fund, or writing books, which are obviously very like, well, we're in charge of those things. (00:34:39): But this is also true, we've been employees in big organizations, I also believe it's true that if you have a boss, and a boss's boss's boss, that you have great insight about what, if you had a window of time, would be the highest leverage thing for you to do. And it might not show up on your OKRs, it might not be on your boss's radar, your boss's boss's boss's boss's radar. You have great intuition, and we want to create space for you to do that thing because you're going to feel better about it, you're going to be more satisfied, and also good things are going to happen.
turns.zh:
别小看这一点，能防止别人占用那段时间。对。别人看了，一看，哦，莱尼已经有安排了。我意识到，好吧，我最好谨慎行事，再请求别人安排事务之前先看看日历。这种默认设置，帮助别人，同意别人在你的空闲时间段安排事务，会削弱我们内心的很多意图。
（00:34:20）：还有一个我们还没提到过的核心观点，我们坚信，如果有机会的话，人们对如何支配时间有着天然的直觉。这才是真正重要的。确实如此。我们谈论运营风投基金、写书，这些显然都是由我们自己掌控的。（00:34:39）但同样真实的是，我们曾在大公司做过员工，我也相信，如果你有上司、上司的上司、上司的上司的上司，你对如果有空闲时间，该做什么事会有很好的洞察力。这些可能不会出现在你的OKR里，可能不会进入你上司的视野、你上司的上司的上司的视野。但你有很强的直觉，我们想为你创造空间去践行这些想法，因为你会因此感觉更好，更满足，而且好事也会发生。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We're spending a lot of time on this highlight, but I think it's because it's so powerful. It's such a simple idea, but so effective. So, just to kind of give people tactical advice for how to actually implement this, just a couple things that I'll summarize. (00:35:23): One is, to pick the highlight, you had a couple of questions I have here, for how to help you pick one for the day. So, you either ask which highlight will bring you the most satisfaction? Or, when I reflect on today, what will bring me the most joy? Maybe that's the same question. But I-
turns.zh: 我们在这部分内容上花了很多时间，但我认为这是因为它太有用了。这是一个很简单的理念，却非常有效。所以，我现在要给出一些切实可行的建议，帮助大家如何实际应用这一理念。（00:35:23）：首先，选择当天的亮点。这里我有几个问题，帮助大家挑选当天的亮点。你可以问自己，哪个亮点能给你带来最大的满足感？或者，当我回顾今天时，什么能给我带来最大的快乐？也许这两个问题是一样的。但我——

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: Slightly different, slightly different.
turns.zh: 稍微不同，稍微不同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Slightly different. That's true. Okay, good.
turns.zh: 稍微不同。这没错。好的，很好。

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: Satisfaction could be like, "I know this thing has to get done, and I got it done."
turns.zh: 满足感可能就像，“我知道这件事必须完成，而且我完成了。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Good point.
turns.zh: 说得好。

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: Joy could be like, "Man, that was great." And they're in the same family, but they're cousins.
turns.zh: 快乐可能就像，“天哪，太棒了。” 它们属于同一类，但又有所不同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great point, great point.
turns.zh: 说得好，说得好。

turns.speaker: John Zeratsky
turns.en: Yeah. And I mentioned, a lot of my highlights, personally, are very much in the urgency or satisfaction camp. They're these big chunky projects. I got it done. I finished that deck. I finished writing that thing. (00:36:11): But I also try to stay attuned to when I need something else in my day, when I need... I need some joy. I need some fun, some play. I need to prioritize going for a run, or going for a walk, or cooking a big dinner. And so, I trust my gut on those things, and I say, "Okay, what's most important to me today is not to be productive, but to do something else." (00:36:39): And sometimes that's the best highlight for me. For other people, maybe that's their highlight every single day. Maybe they work as a... I don't know, I've talked to a lot of people who work in healthcare settings about this. They're a nurse or a doctor, and when they're at work, they're at work. They're not bouncing around between meetings and emails and Zooms. They're on their feet. There's no time to do anything else. So, their highlight is probably something they need to do at the end of the day to unwind, or take care of themselves. (00:37:11): So, you have these three different strategies that we talk about, urgency, satisfaction, and joy, as being three different places you can look for the right highlight for you each day. But ultimately, I think it comes down to just trusting your gut and sort of asking yourself, like you said, "What do I want to look back on and have said, yeah, I'm glad I made time for that"?
turns.zh: 是的。我提到，我个人的很多亮点都属于紧迫感或满足感的范畴。都是些大型的、分阶段的项目。我完成了。我完成了那份演示文稿。我写完了那份报告。（00:36:11）：但我也会留意当天需要什么样的东西，当我需要……我需要一些快乐。我需要一些乐趣，一些玩耍。我需要优先去跑步、散步，或者做一顿丰盛的晚餐。所以，我凭直觉行事，说，“好吧，我今天最重要的不是提高效率，而是做些别的事。”（00:36:39）：有时候，这对我来说就是最好的亮点。对其他人来说，可能每天都是这样的亮点。也许他们在医疗机构工作，比如护士或医生。他们上班时就是工作，没时间在会议、邮件和视频会议之间切换。他们整天都在忙碌。没有时间做其他事。所以，他们的亮点可能是每天结束时放松自己，或者照顾自己的时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So, you touched on the third. So, it's basically, what would give you the most satisfaction? So, in the morning, you essentially ask, or the night before. I think one of you, I forget, because when I was listening to the audiobook, I don't know who's talking. But one of you is like, "I like to do it the day before." Is that right?
turns.zh: 太棒了。所以，你提到了第三个策略。基本上，就是什么能给你带来最大的满足感？所以早上，你可以这样问，或者前一天晚上问。我记得你们中有人说过，“我喜欢前一天晚上就准备好。”对吗？

turns.speaker: John Zeratsky
turns.en: Yeah, that's me.
turns.zh: 对，那是我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Okay.
turns.zh: 好的，好的。

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: That's John talking.
turns.zh: 那是约翰在说话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So, the questions you asked either the night before or in the morning are, "What would give me the most satisfaction today, or the next day? What would give me the most joy? Or what's the most pressing thing that I need to get done?" (00:38:03): So, you do that, and then the advice is either write it on a Post-It... I actually bought these tiny little Post-Its by accident. I was trying to buy regular Post-Its, and they're actually really great for this specific use case, so it's perfect. Write your highlight, stick it on the monitor. (00:38:17): So, that's one way of doing it. The other is stick it in your calendar, where you have focus time. In theory, it's like every day, here's my focus time, where you have the most energy. Is that the general advice?
turns.zh: 好的。所以，你前一天晚上或早上提的问题是：“今天或明天什么事能让我最有满足感？什么事能给我带来最大的快乐？或者我最紧迫需要完成的事是什么？” （00:38:03）：所以，你先这么做，然后建议是把它写在便利贴上……我其实是偶然买了这些小便利贴的。我原本想买普通的便利贴，但它们实际上非常适合这种用途，所以很完美。写下你的重点任务，贴在显示器上。 （00:38:17）：所以，这是一种方法。另一种方法是把它贴在你的日历上，放在你有专注时间的时段。理论上，每天都是这样，这里是我的专注时间，那时你精力最充沛。这是主要的建议吗？

turns.speaker: John Zeratsky
turns.en: Generally, although I think that that's probably more important for a certain kind of highlight. I have focused time most mornings. To be really specific and nerdy about it, Monday, Wednesday and Thursday mornings I have focus time. Tuesday and Friday mornings I have meetings. But on a Thursday night, my highlight might actually be to have friends over and cook dinner. And that's not the same as focus time, but it's this pressure release valve where I'm like, "That's the thing that I want to make sure..." I want to make sure I wrap up email at 5 so that have time to get everything ready, but it's not necessarily that peak energy moment in the way that we might think about being productive or getting things done or getting into that flow state.
turns.zh: 一般来说，虽然我认为这对某种类型的重点任务可能更重要。我大多数早晨都有专注时间。说得更具体、更书生气一点，周一、周三和周四早上我有专注时间。周二和周五早上我有会议。但在周四晚上，我的重点任务可能是邀请朋友来家里做饭。这和专注时间不一样，但这是一个压力释放的阀门，我会想，"这就是我想确保做好的事……" 我想确保在5点前处理完邮件，这样就有时间准备一切，但这不一定是我们所认为的提高效率、完成任务或进入心流状态的那个高能量时刻。

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, there's a lot of ways to do it. So, maybe you just take away, if you're listening to this, is just think about what could be your highlight for today or tomorrow?
turns.zh: 所以，有很多方法可以做到这一点。所以，也许你只要记住，如果你在听这个节目，就想想今天或明天你的重点任务可能是什么？

turns.speaker: John Zeratsky
turns.en: Yeah. And I would say, go one step further and make sure to write it down. Don't just think about it, because there's something really special that happens when you write things down, even if it's on a sticky. Even if it's in your notebook, your journal, even if it's a note on your phone. Take that step as well.
turns.zh: 是的。而且我会说，更进一步，确保把它写下来。不要只是想一想，因为当你把事情写下来时，会发生一些特别的事情，即使写在便利贴上。即使写在你的笔记本、日记里，甚至写在手机的备忘录上。也迈出这一步。

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: Even if you don't see it again, just writing it down is a big deal.
turns.zh: 即使你之后再也看不到它，把它写下来也是一件大事。

turns.speaker: John Zeratsky
turns.en: Yeah, that's a really important point.
turns.zh: 是的，这是一个非常重要的点。

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: I can give you a concrete example of a highlight, and a failed highlight, from yesterday, actually. And so, most days these days, my highlight is around making progress on the book. John alluded to working on a book, and so obviously it's a huge project. I heard it said that if you are writing books, it's like having homework forever. You always feel like there's always more to do. And so, that's mostly been my highlight. (00:40:24): But yesterday, I wanted to prepare for this podcast. I knew that was going to be satisfying, to feel like I was ready. We don't think about talking about Make Time all the time, like we said, it's sort of like a side project for us. So, I wanted to be ready and somewhat coherent. And I knew I'd be satisfied, but I also knew it was urgent. We're going to be doing the recording today. So, that was my highlight. Write that down. "Get ready for podcast." (00:40:50): And I had two focus blocks, one in the morning, one in the afternoon. It should be easy. Focus block number one, kind of just didn't do a good job. I was distracted, I was in my email, I was doing everything that I would say you shouldn't do, I was doing. Feeling down on myself. I've become a loser. I didn't get anything done. (00:41:10): Okay, second focus block. Man, now the pressure's on. I got to do it. And so, I finally get into the zone. And my wife thinks I have a pretty serious case of undiagnosed ADHD, so a lot of it is just, if I really do have a deadline, then I really will click in. So, now I have a deadline. I'm doing it, and I'm making notes, and getting there, but I feel like there's still a ways to go. (00:41:32): And my 12-year-old son bursts into the room, and it was, "Oh gosh, you're invading me right when I'm at peak focus." And he is like, "Hey, I'm going to do one more trip outside to sled in the snow. Do you want to come?" And I'm like, first reaction, "No, absolutely not. I can get this thing done. It's my highlight. This is the one thing I need to do today. I can do it max level of quality if I can just stay in this precious zone of focus." (00:42:02): But then I was like, "Wait a second, what's really going to be the highlight of my day? What's really going to be the highlight, the thing that I might actually remember in the future?" We rarely get snow here. I live on this island in Washington state. We maybe get significant snowfall once every two years. We've only lived here for a few years. He's 12. He loves snow more than anything in the world. He loves snow. But he grew up in California, so he hasn't had many days, and he's 12. He's on the cusp of being a teenager. There's not, maybe, any more days in his life that he's going to want me to get on the sled with him and wrap my arms around him and go down the hill. (00:42:38): I was like, "I got to get out there." So, okay. Pause this, ran outside. We did it. And man, it was magical. And I didn't know we were going to get one more in, because the snow was supposed to be melting already. We went down the hill, we went down the hill, we went... It got dark, we had to stop. But it was so magic. And I remember the very last end of the sled run, and it's like the last one, and he's like, "Man," he's like, "That was a great last sled run. So glad we did it." (00:43:10): And I was like, "Yeah, so glad we did it. It's great." Come back inside, 15 minutes. I try to hustle and get this done. So, I was like, maybe it was like 80% or 75% to where I wanted to be on this. I couldn't check off that highlight as being the most important thing. But because of the framing of, it might be wrong, what am I going to remember, all this stuff, it just felt natural to me to switch modes and say, "Oh my god, that actually is a highlight. That's this thing that's going to be really, really precious. That's where the joy and the satisfaction are most for today." (00:43:47): And still, because I had written down the other thing, I still did it instead of churning on email the entire day. But I screwed up twice, but it still turned out pretty good. So, anyway, that's kind of what it can look like at its best. And a lot of times, it doesn't make that much sense, and a lot of times I miss the special moments, or I miss the key work moments, or the key time when I could have gotten the most done. But I just feel better about it, which is a lot of what this is about. I just feel better about it because I feel more intentional.
turns.zh:
事实上，昨天我能举出一个亮点和一个失败的亮点。大多数日子里，我的亮点就是在书上取得进展。约翰提到在写书，这显然是个大项目。有人说，如果你写书，就好像永远有作业要做，总觉得还有更多事情要做。所以，这基本上就是我的亮点了。（00:40:24）但昨天，我想为这次播客做准备。我知道这会很有成就感，让我感觉准备充分。我们不会一直谈论《抓住时间》这本书，就像我们说的，这对我们来说只是个副业项目。所以，我想做好准备，保持思路清晰。我知道自己会很满足，但我也知道这很紧迫。我们今天就要录制节目了。所以，这就是我的亮点。记下来吧——"为播客做准备"。（00:40:50）我安排了两个专注时间段，一个在上午，一个在下午。本来应该很轻松的。第一个专注时间段，我表现不太好。分心了，一直在处理邮件，干着所有不该做的事。自我感觉很糟糕，觉得自己是个失败者。什么事都没做成。（00:41:10）好吧，到第二个专注时间段了。天哪，现在压力来了。我必须完成任务。终于进入状态了。我妻子觉得我有严重的未确诊的多动症，所以只要有截止日期，我就会集中精力。现在我有截止日期了。我正在做笔记，努力完成，但感觉还有很长的路要走。（00:41:32）这时，我12岁的儿子冲进房间，喊道："天哪，你正处于专注状态，我要打断你了。"他说："嘿，我要再去雪地滑雪橇一次。你想来吗？"我的第一反应是"不行，绝对不行。我能完成这项任务。这是我的亮点。这是我今天必须做的事。如果能保持这种宝贵的专注状态，我就能达到最佳效果。"（00:42:02）但随后我又想："等等，今天真正的亮点是什么？未来可能回想起来最难忘的是什么？"我们这儿很少下雪。我住在华盛顿州的岛上，每两年才下一次大雪。我们搬来这里才几年。他12岁了。他最爱雪。他爱雪。但他在加州长大，所以雪天屈指可数。现在他快成青少年了，可能再也没有机会让我抱着他滑雪橇了。（00:42:38）我说："我必须去。"好吧，让我暂停录音，冲出去。成功了。天哪，太神奇了。本来雪应该已经融化了，但我们又滑了一次。我们滑啊滑...天黑了，不得不停下来。但真的太神奇了。我记得滑雪道的最后一刻，那是最后一次，他说："天哪，这次滑雪太棒了。真高兴我们去了。"（00:43:10）我说："是啊，很高兴我们去了。太棒了。"回到房间，15分钟后，我努力完成工作。可能只完成了80%或75%，但我不能把这个亮点列为最重要的。但因为有了这个框架，它可能会成为最重要的亮点。
或许我做错了什么，但我会记住这一切。对我来说，切换到另一种状态并感叹“天哪，这真是个高光时刻。这件事将成为我最珍视的回忆。今天的快乐与满足感，大多源自此刻。”（00:43:47）  
即便如此，因为我把其他事情写了下来，所以我还是完成了它们，而不是整天埋头处理邮件。不过我也出了两次差错，但最终结果还是不错的。总之，这就是最好的状态。很多时候，事情看起来没什么头绪；很多时候，我错过了那些特别的时刻，或者错过了完成关键工作的机会。但我对此感觉更坦然，这正是这份体验的核心意义所在。我之所以能坦然接受，是因为我做事更有计划性了。

turns.en: Well, it's working out. It all worked out. That's a great story. It reminds me, in your book at some point, I forget who it was of you that had to... And it was like family, writing, Make Time, something else, and then you're like, "Okay, actually Make Time is more important right now than my family," because you just have to get this done, and I wonder if this is a counter.
turns.zh: 嗯，现在看来效果不错。一切都很顺利。这是个很棒的故事。这让我想起，在你的书里有个人物，忘了是谁了，他不得不……你当时说：“这是我目前生活中的优先事项。”然后列举了家庭、写作、《时间管理》之类的，接着你又说：“好吧，其实《时间管理》现在比家庭更重要，因为我必须完成这个任务。”我想知道这是否能成为一个反例。

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: Well, yeah. I mean, I think that part of what people have found useful about Make Time is that John and I come at this from different perspectives. And I have kids. I have a twelve-year-old and a twenty-year-old, sons, and dealing with being a dad is a big part of how I try to figure out how to make sense of what to do. (00:45:13): And John doesn't have kids, and so he has it easy. No, he doesn't, but that's just a different frame of mind. And I think sometimes I read something that people without kids wrote, and I think, "Well yeah, sure. I am sure that's wonderful for you, but what about X-Y-Z?" (00:45:34): And although, I'm sure a lot of people who have more kids, or when they have young kids, it would... But that's a real part of it. And whether it's your family, your significant other, anything that's going on in your life that's not part of your work, there are times when you, on a day, or in a moment, you have to shift those priorities. And it can help to just be this idea of stack-ranking things, and being clear about it, can help you just come to terms with it. "I'm making that decision right now. It makes sense to make right now." Or at least, I can see that I did it, and if it seems like I screwed it up, I'd flip it back. I know where it happened. (00:46:14): A lot of this is just like if you were designing a product or writing code or whatever, you can see that's where the bug happened. I'll just try to fix that line.
turns.zh: 嗯，是的。我觉得人们觉得《时间管理》有用的一个原因是约翰和我从不同角度看待这个问题。（00:45:13）我有孩子。我有两个儿子，一个12岁，一个20岁，日常和他们打交道是我理清生活优先事项的重要方式。约翰没有孩子，所以他比较轻松。不过这只是不同的思维方式。有时候我读到没有孩子的人写的东西，就会想：“嗯，对你来说当然很棒，但X-Y-Z怎么办？” （00:45:34）虽然我相信很多有更多孩子的人，或者孩子还小的时候，会……但这确实是生活的一部分。无论是家庭、伴侣，还是生活中任何与工作无关的部分，总有时候你需要在一天或某个时刻调整优先级。把事情按重要程度排序，明确这一点，对理清思路很有帮助。“我现在要做这个决定，现在做比较合理。”或者至少我能看到自己做了，如果感觉搞砸了，再调整回来。知道问题出在哪里。（00:46:14）这就像设计产品、写代码之类的，能清楚问题出在哪儿。我就试着改那行代码。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I love how real you're getting, and it also reminds me of... We just had a kid. He's seven months old, so I'm going through a lot.
turns.zh: 是啊。你越来越真实了，这也让我想起……我们刚有孩子。他七个月大，所以我现在也经历着很多。

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: Oh, congratulations.
turns.zh: 哦，恭喜。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.en: That's busy times. Seven months old is busy times.
turns.zh: 忙碌的时期。七个月大的孩子就是忙碌的时期。

turns.en: Yeah, that's great.
turns.zh: 是啊，这太棒了。

turns.en: People always told me, told us, when we had kids when they were babies. They're always like, "Oh, just you wait." I just feel like this is a thing that people want to tell other parents. turns.zh: ……对任何开发者免费开放，支持最多100万用户。请访问workos.com了解更多详情。就是workos.com。（00:48:09）：接下来我想谈谈“激光专注力”策略。你可以称之为“如何更好地专注”，而这正是大多数避免分心的实用技巧所在。六年前你出版那本书后，现在这些技巧应该更加完善了。所以让我们快速回顾一些你最喜欢的实用技巧，帮助人们保持专注，以及你实际采用且效果显著的技巧。

turns.speaker: John Zeratsky
turns.en: Yeah, the basic principle with laser is that willpower is never going to win, and there's great research on this, but for now just trust me, you're not going to white-knuckle your way through not looking at Twitter when you're trying to work. So it's all about making it hard, creating barriers to getting distracted. So a few things for me, I'm not on Instagram and I'm not on Facebook. I was on both of those things and I left both of them, I disabled my accounts. I am on Twitter and LinkedIn, but I don't have either of those apps installed on my phone. I stay logged out of those sites on my computer, except for when I want to use them for some specific purpose. (00:49:22): LinkedIn I need to use all the time, because I'm a VC and I have to look people up and stuff, so I found this Chrome plugin, or Chrome extension, I guess is the right word, that disables the feed in LinkedIn. So when I go to LinkedIn.com, it's the search bar at the top but there's no feed, which is amazing because I can use LinkedIn as the phone book and then not get distracted. So those are some of the very, very concrete specific things that I do, all, again, with the goal of putting a speed bump between me and that thing so that if I go, and I don't do this much anymore but I used to, literally my hands on the keyboard would just be like, T-W-I, like Twitter.com, and then you see that log in screen instead of my juicy feed and I'm like, oh yeah, right, okay, I did that on purpose, great, I broke that feedback loop a little bit.
turns.zh: 是的，“激光专注力”的基本原则是意志力永远无法取胜。对此有很多研究，但现在你只需相信我，你没法靠意志力强迫自己在工作时不看Twitter。所以关键在于设置障碍，让分心变得困难。对我来说，我不在Instagram和Facebook上。我曾用过这两个平台，但后来退出并禁用了账号。我在Twitter和LinkedIn上，但手机里没有安装这两个应用。电脑上除非有特定需求，否则一直保持登出状态。（00:49:22）：LinkedIn我需要经常使用，因为我是风投，得查找人脉之类的。所以我找到了一个Chrome插件，或者说扩展程序，能禁用LinkedIn的动态信息流。这样当我访问LinkedIn.com时，顶部只有搜索栏，没有动态信息流，这太棒了，因为我可以把LinkedIn当作人脉名录，同时避免分心。以上就是我采取的具体措施，目的都是在自己和分心事物之间设置障碍。比如我现在不怎么用Twitter了，但以前确实会手动输入Twitter.com，结果看到登录页面而不是动态信息流，然后意识到自己故意这么做的，很棒，打破了这个反馈循环。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I did a similar thing with Twitter/X, where I deleted the app and I just used the mobile website. I think this point of logging out is really powerful, I think people haven't heard that idea as much, because it's not like you can't log in really easily, you just click a couple things and you're back. But to your point, it reminds you, okay, I see, I really shouldn't have done this.
turns.zh: 我在推特/X上也做了类似的操作——我删掉了应用，改用移动版网站。我觉得这个退出登录的功能非常实用，但人们可能不太熟悉这个理念，因为你确实可以轻松登录回来，只需点击几个按钮就能完成。但正如你所说，它能提醒你：好吧，我明白了，其实我不该做这些事。

turns.speaker: John Zeratsky
turns.en: Well, I also signed up for two-factor authentication for everything, not because I care about somebody hacking my account, but because it's another speed bump. Because that way, even if your browser remembers your password, or I use one password, so even if the browser extension is going to fill it in for me, there's still another step, so it's sort of reverse engineering my own distractibility.
turns.zh: 嗯，我还为所有账户启用了双重认证功能，不是因为担心账号被黑，而是因为这又多了一道防护层。这样一来，即便浏览器记住了密码，或者我使用统一密码，即便浏览器扩展程序能自动填充密码，也还是需要额外步骤。这就像在倒逼自己减少分心行为。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That feature that everyone's always talking about that Apple built of the code being automatically there in the keyboard, that's counter to this friction that you've created.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊，这确实有道理。

turns.speaker: John Zeratsky
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, that's true.
turns.zh: 好吧，很有意思的是，我之前也经历过这种情况，结果最后又忍不住重新安装了推特应用。最近我又得和它斗争一番。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so it's interesting is I had this, and then I just like, goddammit I really just want to be on Twitter. And so I just re-installed it again recently, and I need to fight that again.
turns.zh: 嗯，我也经常经历这种循环，在邮箱使用上更是如此。杰克，你手机上还是没有邮箱，对吧？

turns.speaker: John Zeratsky
turns.en: Well, I go through cycles like that too, and I go through that a lot with email. Jake, you still don't have email on your phone, is that right?
turns.zh: 对啊，如果我装了邮箱，现在肯定在开会时躺在地上查看邮件了。

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: No, I would be on the floor checking email right now on this call if I did, on the floor.
turns.zh: 不然我现在肯定躺在地上查看邮件了。

turns.speaker: John Zeratsky
turns.en: I used to do that, Jake inspired me a long time ago to remove email from my phone, and so for years and years that's been my default. But more recently I've had more reasons to install it, mostly related to travel, if I'm on the go and I just want to stay on top of things. And something that Jake and I have talked about a lot is you go through these different cycles of, hey, I need this thing, or I want this thing, and then part of the reflect step, part of paying attention and reflecting on how it's going is to recognize, oh wow, I've actually been spending a lot of time on email on my phone, or a lot of time on Twitter, maybe I'll just uninstall it for a while. Maybe I'll just reset and do that for a while. And then there'll be some other thing that happens that causes you to reinstall it, and that's totally fine, because you're being deliberate about it and you're paying attention, rather than saying it has to always be this way forever and it's set in stone.
turns.zh: 我以前也这么做过，杰克很久以前就启发我把手机邮箱卸载掉，之后好多年我一直保持这个习惯。但最近我又有更多安装邮箱的理由，主要是出于旅行需求，比如在路上想及时处理邮件时用到它。我们常讨论的一个点是，你会经历各种循环——比如觉得自己需要某个功能，或者想用某个功能——然后反思阶段、关注并反思进展的过程，就是意识到：哇，我在手机上花了太多时间看邮件，或者刷推特，或许我该卸载一阵子。然后又会有新情况促使你重新安装，但这完全没关系，因为你是在有意识地控制局面，而非认为事情必须永远如此、一成不变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a great tip of just coming back to it, not feeling like you're defeated, it's like, all right, let's try this again.
turns.zh: 重新审视这个过程，别觉得自己失败了，而是想：好吧，再试一次。

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: Yeah, I think a big part of it is if you can experience the feeling of not having it on your phone. Like I'm old enough to have lived in a world building products where there were no smartphones, and we got a lot done back then, things happened. I mean, for God's sake, they designed the first iPhone without being able to use iPhones while they did it, you can do a lot. So this idea that we have to have it or everything's going to fall apart, that's just not true for 99.99999% of everyone. (00:53:16): It's interesting to see what it feels like if you delete all of the infinity pools off of your phone, and this is something I did out of rage at myself in 2012. It was another situation where I was with my kids, who were much younger at the time, and I was spending time with them, we're playing wooden trains, and all of a sudden my son's like, "Dad, dad, dad, dad, dad," and I'm like, "God, what?" And I didn't even realize it but I was on my phone, and I don't even remember what I was doing, email or something, but I think I told him, he's like, "What's on your phone?" Because to him, he was like, we're doing something really fun, so if you're on your phone it must be something really cool, maybe it would be a cool thing to share, because this is great, so it must be another great thing. He wasn't trying to shame me or anything. (00:54:06): And I was all defensive, I'm like, "Well, I need to do this for work," which was, I think, my internal monologue of why I was doing this thing that actually was just a really low-friction dopamine hit. And then I thought, God, this is not what I wanted, this is not why I worked so hard today so I would get done with my work so I could be home in time to do this before my kids go to bed. And I was like, screw this, so I just started deleting things on my phone, and I deleted email and I deleted Facebook and I deleted this, everything that had an infinity pool, everything that had an infinite amount of content. News is like this, anything streaming. (00:54:44): When we wrote this book, it came out in 2018, I think we said we thought it was going to get worse, and it has. But at that point in time there was really Netflix, and now there's all these streaming services. At that point in time there was Instagram and Facebook, but now there's TikTok, the best part of every video available instantly right here. This stuff, it only gets harder to resist. When you clear all that stuff off of your phone, it's painful, the idea of deleting all this stuff, and each time the phone's going to ask you, "This is going to delete all the data and settings, are you sure you want to do that?" It doesn't want you to. And when you do that though, what does that feel like? And it's usually a feeling of discomfort, but also relief that I don't have to check this, this thing, I don't have to check it, I don't have to. (00:55:34): And if you've ever felt like your phone was in the Lord of the Rings, how Bilbo, I guess, yeah, Lord of the Rings, they want to put their hand in their pocket and touch the ring, or put the ring on without even knowing it, Frodo's like, "I didn't even realize I did it." That's what this thing is like. And when you take those off, just that feeling of relief is, to me, so powerful, that having done this for a decade now, and yeah, there's exceptions, like I'm traveling, God, I have to check my email for X reason, and I install it and I check it. And then it automatically, because I'm aware of it, I'll just feel this static. (00:56:11): There's this notion of attention residue, and I think the researcher who coined this term is Sophie Leroy from the University of Washington. Anyway, you can look that up, I think I learned about that from Cal Newport. But this idea says, it makes a lot of sense, that you pay attention to some things and they just stick in your head and they create this static, those apps just create this static. The idea of email being on my phone and accessible at any time creates a discomfort, a disquiet that now that I've seen it and felt what it's like to not have it, I could not imagine experiencing it. (00:56:44): You do give some things up. You're not going to be as responsive. John and I don't have as many Twitter followers as we'd have if we used Twitter. There are these things that you look at other people, and I just saw a post on LinkedIn because I haven't used plug-in yet, but I looked on this post and it was a colleague that I used to have and she was saying, "Yeah, I posted a few tweets last year and a couple of them went viral and I gained 30,000 followers." And I was like, man, all I have is 30,000 followers, and that was from years and years ago, I thought I was a pretty big deal, oh jeez, maybe I should... And I was like, oh God, don't do it, because I know when I'm doing it, then I'll be thinking about it all the time and the attention residue will spoil my life. (00:57:28): So yeah, anyway, sorry, that's just a rant, but you should try it. The distraction-free phone thing is just worth trying, if you can take off everything, if not just try taking off the thing that's your kryptonite. What's the thing that is the hardest for you to resist, sucks your attention the most, makes you feel not good? Take it off for, try it for a day, or try it for two hours, just to feel that feeling. And then once you've felt the feeling you'll always know, I could release that, and I think that's powerful.
turns.zh:
是啊，我觉得关键在于，你能否体验到手机不在身边的感觉。比如，我年纪够大了，经历过没有智能手机的时代，那时我们也能把事情做好，事情也能推进。天啊，他们设计第一代iPhone时，根本没法用iPhone来做设计，但他们还是做出了很多东西。所以那种认为非得时刻拿着手机，否则一切都会崩塌的想法，对99.99999%的人来说根本不成立。（00:53:16）：看看把手机里所有信息流都删掉会是什么感觉，这事儿我在2012年干过，当时我因为对自己生气才这么做。当时我和孩子们在一起，他们还很小，我陪他们玩木头火车游戏，突然我儿子喊：“爸爸，爸爸，爸爸，爸爸，爸爸，”我当时就想：“天哪，什么事？”结果我甚至没意识到自己在玩手机，也不记得在干什么，可能是查看邮件之类的，但我记得自己跟他说：“手机里有什么啊？”对他来说，他觉得我们在做很有趣的事，所以如果你在玩手机，那肯定是在做很酷的事，或许能分享出来，因为这事儿很棒，那肯定还有其他很棒的东西。他不是要羞辱我什么的。（00:54:06）：我当时特别防御，说：“嗯，我工作需要用。”这应该是我当时的内心独白，解释自己为什么要这么做，而实际上这不过是低阻力多巴胺奖励罢了。然后我突然意识到，这根本不是我想要的，这也不是我今天拼命工作的目的，就是为了能及时回家陪孩子睡觉。于是我说：去他的，我要把手机上的东西都删掉。我删掉了邮件，删掉了Facebook，删掉了所有带有信息流的东西。新闻推送也是这样，任何流媒体内容都是如此。（00:54:44）：我们写这本书的时候，2018年出版的，我们当时觉得情况会越来越糟，现在确实如此。但当时只有Netflix，现在则涌现了各种流媒体平台。当时只有Instagram和Facebook，现在又有了TikTok，所有视频都能即时呈现。这些东西越来越让人难以抗拒。当你把手机里所有东西都清空时，那种痛苦感太强烈了，删除所有数据和设置的提示会反复出现，它根本不想让你这么做。但当你真的这么做后，那种解脱感又让人觉得很棒。（00:55:34）：如果你曾觉得自己的手机像《指环王》里的比尔博，我猜对，就是《指环王》里那个人，他想把手伸进口袋摸戒指，或者不知不觉戴上戒指，弗罗多会说：“我甚至都没意识到自己这么做了。”这就是手机的魔力。当你卸载这些应用时，那种解脱感对我来说太强烈了。坚持了十年下来，当然也有例外情况，比如出差时因为某种原因需要查邮件，我就安装好邮箱再查。但即便如此，因为我心里有数，总会感觉到那种静电感。
谁创造了这个术语？是来自华盛顿大学的索菲·勒罗伊。反正你可以去查证一下，我记得是从卡尔·纽波特那里了解到的。但这个观点很有道理——你会注意到某些事物，它们就会深深印在你的脑海里，形成一种干扰。那些应用程序就是在制造这种干扰。手机上的邮件随时待命的设定会带来一种不适感，一种不安。现在我亲身经历过没有邮件的状态，深知其带来的影响，简直难以想象还能继续忍受它。（00:56:44）：你确实会放弃一些东西。你的响应速度会变慢。约翰和我在推特上的粉丝比使用推特时要少很多。看看别人的情况吧——我刚在领英上看到一个帖子，因为我还没用过插件，但我看了这个帖子，发现是我以前的一个同事。她说：“去年我发了几条推特，其中有两条火了，收获了3万粉丝。”我当时就想，天啊，我现在只有3万粉丝，而且还是多年前的事了。我还以为自己很了不起，天哪，也许我该……但我又想，哦不，千万别这么做，因为我知道一旦开始用这些应用，我就总会去想它们，注意力残留会毁了我的生活。（00:57:28）：所以是的，抱歉，这只是我的牢骚，但你应该试试看。无干扰手机模式真的值得一试，如果你能卸载所有应用；如果不行，就先从最让你上瘾的那个开始。哪个东西最难抵抗，最容易吸走你的注意力，让你感觉糟糕？试试看一天或者两个小时，感受那种感觉。一旦你体会到那种感觉，你就永远知道自己能放下它，我觉得这很重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I think when you delete it, it's important to know nothing's being deleted when you're deleting the app, you can reinstall it, you log in, it's all the same.
turns.zh: 我觉得当你删除某个应用时，重要的是要知道删除应用并不意味着数据被永久删除。你可以重新安装它，重新登录，一切照旧。

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: It's all the same, that's an important point. They make it sound like, oh my God, this is a big deal. It's not.
turns.zh: 这一点很重要。他们把这事说得好像天都要塌下来似的。其实没那么严重。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, just have to remember your password or Google auth, or whatever you're using. This metaphor of The Lord of the Rings and the ring is so good for how it feels to just say, I'm just going to check Twitter, what's the problem, I'm just going to check it again, I'll just check it, check it. That's so good. And then in Lord of the Rings, the way they resist the ring is they hide it, they put it somewhere else, they give it to Frodo to take it, right? That's the same solution, it's just like, I can't get access to it, it's over there.
turns.zh: 是啊，只要记得密码或者Google账号之类的。用《指环王》里的隐喻来比喻这个问题再合适不过了——就像你想说"我只是去看看推特，有什么大不了的？"但其实你越看越上瘾，最后只能说"算了，先退出再说"。《指环王》里的故事是，人们如何抵制魔戒的诱惑。他们把魔戒藏起来，交给弗罗多，让他带走。这和我们处理手机应用的思路是一样的，就是把诱惑转移到别处。

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: Right, right. Yeah, you got to be like Gandalf. Even if that ring would do great things for you, you got to give it to Frodo for a while, maybe show up at the end with an eagle.
turns.zh: 对，对。你得像甘道夫那样。即使魔戒能给你带来好处，你也得暂时交给弗罗多，最后再骑着鹰出现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just too eerie, yeah, yeah, the eagle.
turns.zh: 太不可思议了，没错，鹰。

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: Scoop them up.
turns.zh: 把它们都收起来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, oh man. So the key tips here are find the apps that are sucking your attention, could be Twitter, could be LinkedIn, could be your email, and delete them and/or log out of them. What else?
turns.zh: 是啊，可惜了。关键是要找出那些让你分心注意力的应用，比如推特、领英、邮箱，然后删掉它们或者退出登录。还有别的建议吗？

turns.speaker: John Zeratsky
turns.en: There's a few tactics that Jake and I both use that are related to TV, watching TV, and a really simple one, which is also kind of a luxury one, but I think there are ways to do it that are pretty universal, is just not having a TV in your main living space. Again, not having the default be like, I'm home, the TV is on, what are we watching? And so for me and my wife, that's always been the TV is just in a different room. And Jake, do you use a projector where if you want to watch something you have to get it out, set it up, and make a decision to watch something?
turns.zh: 杰克和我都用过几个和电视相关的技巧。比如看电视，控制自己不被动地打开电视，问自己"回家后看什么？"对我和妻子来说，电视一直在另一个房间。杰克，你用的是投影仪吗？要看电影得先把设备拿出来，组装好再决定看什么？

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp

嗯，首先是设定预期，然后再增加一项策略。设定预期和减少邮箱收件量是两个主要与邮件和消息相关的技巧。设定预期就是和同事沟通，或者在邮件签名中说明情况。比如：“我每天检查邮件两次，以此提升专注力”或者“我每天检查一到两次邮件，具体次数取决于我正在处理的重要项目”。这样简单的提示能让对方意识到你的回复速度不会太快，同时又不显得生硬。

（01:09:11）你可以把这段话写进自动回复邮件，比如：“我目前正专注于一个重要项目，无法及时回复邮件。若事务紧急，请直接发消息。”这样比起传统的离线通知更自然，也更符合现代工作节奏。

（01:09:58）关键在于“因为”这个理由。书中提到一项研究，人们会编造虚假借口，比如“因为要排队打印文件”之类。研究发现，只要加上“因为……所以”的解释，人们就更容易接受延迟回复的请求。这说明我们对理由的依赖心理很强。告诉对方原因能让他们更容易接受你的请求，同时也能减轻自己的心理压力。

（01:10:46）第二个策略是减少邮箱收件量。每天只查看一两次邮件，或者减少查看次数，但同时保持回复效率。这样能让整个处理邮件的循环更顺畅。快速回复邮件会导致邮件量激增，放慢节奏则能控制邮件堆积。

You can imagine all the app logos, they're just kind of vibrating right around my head. (01:14:07): They're right there and touching any one of them, it's like they're little pieces of candy. It's all going to feel good. There's this really good meal, five to 10 feet away is this great sandwich, but these little pieces of candy are right in my face and it's going to be hard to resist just popping a little Sour Patch Kid or Laffy Taffy in my mouth, but if I could push them away, if I can just push them far enough away so that there is far away or farther away than the sandwich, I'm going to eat the sandwich. Once there's space, you'll want to do the thing that's most important. It's just it's hard because the candy is right in our face.
turns.zh: 可能是在咖啡店，找不到wifi密码，却有种令人惊喜的感觉。又或许是去没有wifi的公园，随便哪种地方，只要你无法获取这些干扰信息就行。如果实在忍不住想删除所有应用，那就把手机留在家里。真是太棒了。太棒了。这样你就无需再与这些诱惑抗争了。（01:13:46）我常想起一个画面：我面前有待完成的任务。就在眼前。这件我想做的事，但它离我五英尺或十英尺远，而就在我身边，不断振动的是所有应用的图标。（01:14:07）它们就在眼前，随便点开一个，都像糖果一样诱人。这些糖果般的诱惑实在难以抗拒。但如果我能把它们推得足够远，远到比三明治更远的距离，我就能专心吃三明治了。迈克，如果你能用这种方法抵御这些干扰，你就能进入专注模式，轻而易举。只要有空间，你就会想去做最重要的事。关键是这些糖果般的诱惑实在太诱人了。

turns.en: Such a good metaphor. You also have this metaphor of Odysseus sailing past the sirens. If folks know that story where there was a siren, I don't know, cliff thing where he's just sailing.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Man, what a character to play. Yeah. And in that story, he wanted to experience these sirens who nobody could resist, but he forced his sailors to tie him to the ship and not allow him to do anything, even though he's like, "Let me go. I need to go there." Because everyone crashed into the sirens. turns.zh: 天哪，演这个角色可真难。是啊。在那个故事里，他想去体验那些让人无法抗拒的塞壬，但他却强迫水手们把他绑在船上，不让他做任何事——尽管他一直说：“放开我，我得去那儿。”因为所有人都被塞壬吸引住了。反正我讲得挺糟糕的，但我想关键点还是反复强调：你不能依赖意志力去抵抗身边那些让人心动的诱惑，你必须建立一套系统来规避这些诱惑。

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: I think there's this notion that we will use willpower maybe comes from the fact that some people can, maybe some people are just using willpower or they're on Twitter, they're on Instagram, they're on TikTok, they're on Facebook, they're doing all these things, and they're also functioning just fine, or at least what we see from the outside is just fine. But maybe internally too, it's fine. (01:16:07): It just seems that everybody I actually talk to and certainly my personal experiences, all that stuff makes me feel bad and actually undercuts my ability to do the things that are meaningful. The meaningful contributions I can make through my work or through my life, whatever. They're all undermined and undercut by the bad feelings and the distraction that come from all of social media, all of the news and almost all of my email. And so if that's true for anybody, if it's even remotely true for us, we have to just radically rethink what we're doing. (01:16:42): This thing, I think we basically are steered toward becoming reaction machines and this notion of, "I'm going to have an empty inbox. I'm going to do every task. I'm going to be a fast responder, I'm going to be in every meeting. I'm going to do that because I want to help other people, and that's the way it works." I think this desire to be helpful is a big driver of it. I think we want to alleviate our stress and other people's stress, and that seems like the right way to do it. It's candy. Some of the stuff is candy and easy. (01:17:12): We also see this modeled by people in power, so like CEOs and bosses, it works for them because they're applying their influence through being constantly reactive and being in meetings all the time. That's just how they do what they do. That's how they apply their influence. But even for them, I think it has limits as a way to apply influence. At the bare minimum for the rest of us. And for those of us who again, I think is the vast, vast majority for whom all of these things create problems and we're not able to easily willpower and self-esteem manage all this stuff, if we're a reaction machine, we're not doing meaningful work, no Project A's and we're not really alive as humans. We're just chat bots. So it's worth experimenting if you don't want to live your life out as a chatbot.
turns.zh: 我觉得人们对意志力的依赖，可能源于某些人确实能做到这一点——或许他们只是在用意志力抵抗诱惑，比如在推特、Instagram、抖音、脸书上刷手机，同时还能正常生活，或者至少从外表看没问题。但也许他们内心深处也备受煎熬。（01:16:07）：但我发现，我接触的大多数人，包括我自己的经历，都让我感觉很糟糕，这些东西严重削弱了我做有意义事情的能力。无论是通过工作还是生活做出有意义的贡献，都被社交媒体带来的负面情绪、新闻推送和邮件通知所侵蚀。如果这对任何人适用，哪怕只是一点点，我们都必须彻底重新思考我们的行为模式。（01:16:42）：我觉得我们基本上被导向成为反应机器，遵循“保持收件箱空”、“完成所有任务”、“快速回复”、“参加所有会议”的模式。我们总以为这样能帮助他人，但这其实是糖果陷阱。有些东西确实很轻松。（01:17:12）：我们还看到权势人物以此为范本，比如CEO和老板们，他们通过不断反应、频繁开会来施展影响力。这就是他们的行事之道。但即便对他们来说，这种施加影响力的方式也有局限性。至少对我们普通人如此。对绝大多数人来说，这些东西都会引发问题，我们无法仅靠意志力和自尊来应对所有事。如果我们成为反应机器，就无法开展有意义的工作，无法完成A级项目，也无法真正活出自我。我们不过是聊天机器人。所以如果你不想把自己活成聊天机器人，还是值得尝试探索新方法的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think the point you made there around the feeling is just a really important point that even if you feel really productive enough and you're getting things done, is if you're feeling bad, it's still an important thing to focus on. It's called mailmanhq.com. It shuts off your Gmail for periods of time. So you could say, "Only allow my email through at these times of day." turns.zh: 我认为你提到的关于情绪感受的观点非常重要。即使你觉得自己效率很高、完成了任务，但如果情绪低落，关注这一点仍然至关重要。比如，你是否在花时间做自己想做的事？你还让我想起了一个应用程序，我简单提一下，相信大家会喜欢的。我不知道你们是否听说过它，叫MailmanHQ.com。它可以暂时关闭Gmail功能。比如你可以设定每天特定时段允许邮件接收，这样就能批量处理邮件了。

turns.zh: 好的。接下来我们要探讨这个框架的最后两个部分——激发活力和反思，然后花点时间讲讲Sprint，让大家了解这个方法的核心内容。特别是那些没读过这本书的人。

turns.speaker: John Zeratsky
turns.en: So to replay the system overall highlight is about the thing you want to make time for today. The most important thing today, laser is about creating barriers to distraction so that you have much your energy or as much of your attention as possible to focus on your highlight on that one thing. Energize is sort of like a booster to laser. (01:19:29): It's sort of like the big idea is that our brains and bodies are connected and our ability to pay attention and to focus and to do those things that we care about only works when we are well and we have slept, we have eaten well, we have exercised, we have talked to other people the right amount, not too much, not too little and so we put this as part of the make time framework because we don't think you should go crazy, try a million biohacker type of things, but we do think it's worth applying this same philosophy of pay attention to what's working, what's not, have a system, try some new things, pay attention to those things, run these experiments. We think it's worth doing that for your health, for your energy as well, because it really does make a difference.
turns.zh: 所以，整个框架的核心要点在于，确定今天你想为之腾出时间的重点。今天最重要的事，激光专注的核心在于设置抗干扰屏障，这样你就能尽可能多地将精力和注意力集中在当天的重点任务上。激发活力有点像激光专注的助推器。（01:19:29）：其核心理念是，我们的大脑和身体是相连的，只有在身体健康、睡眠充足、饮食健康、锻炼得当、与人交流适度（不过多也不过少）的情况下，我们才能专注于真正重要的事情。因此，我们将这部分纳入腾出时间框架，因为我们不认为你应该去尝试无数种极客养生法，但我们认为值得应用同样的理念：关注有效的方法，识别无效的做法，建立系统，尝试新事物，持续优化。无论是出于健康还是提升效率的考虑，这都非常值得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe share one or two tips there real quick for people to energize to create a little more energy during their day?
turns.zh: 或许你能快速分享一两个小技巧，帮助大家在一天中激发更多能量？

turns.speaker: John Zeratsky
turns.en: In the year since we wrote the book and as my life has just continued to change and I've gotten a little bit older, I've realized that sleep is probably the single most important thing. I mentioned earlier, not having my phone in the bedroom, no TV in the bedroom, hopefully that goes without saying, but just being able to really construct an environment that allows me to sleep. I started wearing an eye mask recently.
turns.zh: 自从我们写完那本书以来，一年过去了，随着生活继续变化，我也逐渐变老，我意识到睡眠可能是最重要的一件事。我之前提到过，卧室里不放手机，不看电视，希望这是不言而喻的，但真正能营造睡眠环境也很重要。比如，我最近开始戴眼罩了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I do that.
turns.zh: 我也这么做。

turns.speaker: John Zeratsky
turns.en: Yeah, really helps me fall asleep and stay asleep and then the other thing is exercise is a big source of energy for me, but I realized that I was making excuses about why I didn't need to or shouldn't exercise in any given day. So even though this is not what we recommended in the book specifically, I ended up signing on with a personal trainer so that I have accountability, I have a schedule, I have somebody who's thinking about what I need that's not just me and those two things have kind of been the pillars of how I build energy over the last few years.
turns.zh: 是啊，这确实能帮助我入睡并保持睡眠状态。另外，对我来说，锻炼是获取能量的重要来源，但我意识到自己总在找借口说某天不需要或不该锻炼。所以尽管书中并未特别推荐这种做法，我最终还是找了一位私人教练，这样既能督促自己，也能制定锻炼计划。毕竟，教练会根据我的需求制定训练方案，而不只是我自己考虑这些因素。过去几年里，这两项举措始终是我提升精力的核心支柱。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I use this app called Future, I'm a investor, quick disclaimer, but it's basically a personal trainer through an app that's like a real person that helps you design a workout for you, and then they give you the workout on the app and you just follow the instructions and that's the thing that got you working out three times a week.
turns.zh: 我用了一个叫Future的应用程序，我是它的投资者，先做个免责声明。不过说实话，这个应用就像一位真实的私人教练，能帮你设计锻炼计划，然后在应用里提供训练指导。你只需按照指示执行，这就是我能每周锻炼三次的关键。

turns.en: Nice. Yeah.
turns.zh: 不错啊。

turns.en: That's awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Jake Knapp
turns.en: Reflect is just simply the act of looking back on the day and treating the day. It wasn't marble gravestone of your successes or failures, it's just a experiment that you ran. What happened in the experiment? Taking note of it in that lens, what did it look like? There's a template in our book that has some questions you can answer, but really it's pretty simple. (01:22:44): If you write down your highlight in the morning or the night before, if you're draw it and you stick it somewhere visible, then at the end of the day you just look at it and just like, "Okay, did that happen or did that not happen?" If you stick it somewhere visible, you won't even have to do anything. You'll just come across it and you'll know if did that happen or not? So that's the simplest part of it is writing it down, sticking it will create a reflection loop for you. (01:23:14): Another thing that I think is quite powerful at the end of the day is to write down, keep a notebook by the side of the bed and write down one or two or three things that you are grateful for during the day, just like a simple gratitude journal. And you'll start, this keeps you in this frame of mind of what was cool today, what happened that was satisfying or joyful, what brought me joy and then if you start the day thinking about what you'd like to happen and then you look back and say, "What was great?" Your brain is just starting to look for those good things. Look for those big highlights, and that's a great way to live your life day to day saying, "This is what I hope will happen. This is what did happen. Now I'm more tuned into what it might happen tomorrow. Oh, now I'm more tuned into what happened today." And again, and it's just a really nice loop. So was there a connection between what you hoped would happen? Did you manage to do your highlight? If so, what helped you do it? What worked or didn't work? What made it hard? It might be an energy thing that suggests a tweak to when you drink coffee or if you take a walk or whatever. It might've been a focus thing. So maybe I'll try another barrier for this thing because that undercut me. Whatever it is, it's just basically, in summary, curiosity about your day instead of self-judgment about your day.
turns.zh: 反思其实就是回顾一天并审视这一天。它不是刻画你成功或失败的纪念碑，而是你进行的一次实验。实验中发生了什么？从这个视角看，它呈现出怎样的面貌？我们的书中有一个模板，里面有一些问题供你回答，但其实这很简单。（01:22:44）：如果你在早上或前一晚写下当天的亮点，如果你把它画下来并贴在显眼的地方，那么一天结束时，你只需看看它，问自己：“好吧，这件事发生了还是没有发生？”如果你把它贴在显眼的地方，你甚至无需做任何额外努力。当你再次看到它时，就能知道它是否真的发生了。所以最简单的部分就是把它写下来，贴起来，这会为你创造一个反思循环。（01:23:14）：我认为一天结束时做另一件事也很有力量，那就是在床边放一本笔记本，写下一天中感恩的1-2件事，就像一个简单的感恩日记。你会开始回想今天有什么很棒的事，发生了什么令人满足或快乐的事，什么带给我欢乐的事。然后你开始新的一天，想着希望发生什么事，再回头看看：“有什么很棒的事呢？”你的大脑就会开始寻找这些美好的事物。寻找那些重大的亮点，这是过好每一天的好方法。说“这是我希望发生的事。这是实际发生的事。现在我更关注明天可能会发生什么。哦，现在我更关注今天发生了什么。”再说一次，这是一个非常好的循环。所以你希望发生的事和实际发生的之间有什么联系吗？你成功完成了你的亮点吗？如果是这样，什么帮助了你？什么有效，什么无效？什么让它变得困难？可能是能量问题，比如调整咖啡饮用时间或散步时间之类的。也可能是专注力问题。那么也许我会为这件事尝试另一个策略，因为它让我受挫了。无论是什么，总之，就是对自己的一天保持好奇心，而不是自我评判。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think we've covered Make Time and tons of depth if people want to practice these things, highly recommend getting the book.
